title: Blood in the Front of the Eye

patient.name: Mr Daniel Wong
patient.presenting_complaint: Hit in the right eye by a squash ball an hour ago; now sees blurred and there is blood visible in the front of the eye

history.hpc: Mr Daniel was hit in the right eye by a squash ball. He says: 'The ball hit my eye, now my vision blur and I see like got blood inside the front part.' There is a visible layer of blood in the anterior chamber (hyphaema). He has eye ache and light sensitivity. Blunt trauma with hyphaema is a serious injury that needs prompt assessment and rest.
history.social_hx: Plays squash; was not wearing protective eyewear.

iop.right: may be raised; measure gently/per protocol once it is safe

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right eye: visible blood layer in the anterior chamber (hyphaema); conjunctival redness
examination_findings.fundus: View may be limited by the hyphaema; for doctor

investigations.front_line_action: Recognise a hyphaema (blood in the anterior chamber) after blunt trauma as a serious injury (a total hyphaema is Category 2; a small hyphaema Category 3) needing prompt doctor assessment. Avoid any pressure on the eye, keep the patient upright and resting, and escalate. Watch for an associated rise in eye pressure.

diagnosis: Traumatic hyphaema (blood in the anterior chamber) from blunt injury — a serious eye injury that can be complicated by raised IOP and re-bleeding. The PSA competency is recognising the hyphaema, escalating promptly, advising rest, and avoiding pressure on the eye; medical management is the doctor's.

immediate: Recognise the blood layer in the anterior chamber as a hyphaema from blunt trauma
Escalate promptly to the doctor (total hyphaema is Category 2; small hyphaema Category 3)
Keep the patient upright/seated and resting; advise minimal movement and no straining
Avoid any pressure on the eye; do not instil drops without the doctor's order
Measure VA; defer/measure IOP gently only as protocol allows, watching for raised pressure
Document the mechanism, time, the hyphaema, VA, and the escalation
follow_up: Doctor to assess the hyphaema and IOP and arrange management/monitoring
Advise rest with head elevated and avoidance of strenuous activity as directed
Check tetanus status if any associated surface injury; document on the record
patient_education: Explain that the blood inside the eye needs the doctor to review promptly
Advise him to rest, stay upright, and avoid bending, straining, or rubbing the eye
Explain the importance of follow-up to watch for pressure rise or re-bleeding
Advise protective eyewear for racquet sports in future

key_points: Establishes the blunt trauma mechanism (squash ball) and time
Identifies the visual blurring and visible blood in the eye
Asks about pain and light sensitivity
Notes the lack of protective eyewear
Recognises the anterior chamber blood as a hyphaema
Measures VA and assigns appropriate triage urgency
Avoids pressure on the eye and defers/gentle IOP per protocol
Documents mechanism, time, hyphaema, and VA
Identifies traumatic hyphaema as a serious injury
Knows total hyphaema is Category 2 and small hyphaema Category 3
Recognises the risk of raised IOP and re-bleeding
Knows medical management is the doctor's role
Advises rest, upright posture, and no straining or rubbing
Avoids drops/pressure without the doctor's order
Documents the injury and escalation accurately
